fieldMarks: The only deer in which both sexes grow antlers; bulls' antlers are large and massive, cows' much shorter, slender and irregular.
Large, concave hooves that splay widely and large, set-back dewclaws, leaving big rounded tracks.
Autumn bulls: rich brown or grey coat with white neck, rump and feet, often a white flank stripe, and a white throat-to-chest fringe.
Woodland caribou are the largest and darkest; barren-ground somewhat smaller and lighter; Peary caribou small and light-coloured.
Adult bulls average about 350-400 lb (159-182 kg), cows 175-225 lb (Alaska).
behavior: Large herds migrate up to 400 miles (640 km) between summer and winter ranges; smaller herds may not migrate.
Lichens are the main winter food, located by smell and dug out of snow with the hooves; summer diet is willow leaves, sedges, flowering plants and mushrooms.
Usually quiet but may give a loud snort; cows and calves call constantly around calving.
Bulls shed antlers in November-December after the rut; each herd uses a distinct calving area.
habitat: Woodland caribou use boreal forest, bogs and fens, and in western mountains move between forested winter range and alpine tundra; barren-ground caribou spend much or all of the year on tundra; Peary caribou live on Arctic islands.
range: In Canada from the U.S. border to northern Ellesmere Island and from British Columbia and Yukon to Newfoundland, with the southern limit receding northward. Alaska holds 31 herds, mostly barren-ground caribou plus one small woodland herd (Chisana).
